The work

Eight formats, four audiences: retail staff and dealers, the general public, journalists, and my own team. The figures are mine; where I cannot count something I say so.

In-store workshops for the public

25 sessions over 4 years · 30–35 people each · one hour · free to attend

The purpose was to bring people into the Samsung Experience Stores and let them get comfortable there. They came to learn something real — mobile photography, painting, or a particular device feature — and to spend an hour actually using the phones rather than being sold one.

People registered through the official page and were invited to a one-hour class. Each session ran a competition on that day's subject, and everyone left with a certificate and a prize.

The curriculum and the materials were built in-house. I delivered a share of the sessions; the training team delivered the rest.

exercises & activitiesgamificationtraining deliveryretention

Pre-launch dealer seminars, taught as role play

One-day seminars before each flagship launch · for the stores carrying pre-orders

Ahead of a flagship launch and its pre-order window, the stores taking pre-orders got a full-day seminar. It was not delivered as a presentation. It was role play: staff practised the actual customer conversation, and at the end of each round they had to run it themselves. That is how we knew they could do it, rather than assuming.

A short test followed. I kept it deliberately gentle — the point was a review we did together, not pressure. Staff who are anxious about being caught out stop asking the questions that reveal what they do not know.

role playssimulationsperformance criteriasales processes

Online workshops

4 titles · 10+ broadcasts · 10–15 learners each

Recorded once under the Galaxy Workshop brand, then broadcast to registered learners with the feel of a live class, so one recording could run again and again.

I was the instructor and responsible for the presentation. The studio space and the filming were handled by an agency.

The training platform

500 → 4,000+ monthly active users · 100% of the transition target

COVID ended in-person seminars, and the territory could not reach the global Samsung Plus platform. The training function lost its delivery channel and its tooling in the same year, so we built our own — a local training platform plus a standing video library for retail staff.

A full learning system rather than a video shelf: courses, live webinars, exams with a pass mark per course, and a certificate issued on passing. Points from completing a course fed a rewards draw.

The library covered what moves a sale — conflict resolution, empathic customer behaviour, selling to different personality types, service delivery. The material and the assessment that followed it were written in-house.

The training channel

NDA press briefings

One a year for 4 years · ~30 journalists and tech influencers each · online

Closed pre-launch briefings on the flagship lines — Fold and S series — for press and technology influencers, before the public announcement. HQ shared the source material; I localised and rebuilt it for the room, and the technical explanation was mine to give.

Journalists write in the days after launch. If they have not understood the product properly beforehand, the coverage is wrong and cannot be corrected afterwards.

audience needsfacilitationlocalisation

Launch events — training zone and game zone

5 events · game zones designed with an agency, signed off by me

At public launch events I owned the training area and the game zone — the interactive part where visitors actually touch the product. I defined the activities a visitor would do, worked with the agency on the game design, and approved what shipped.

It is the clearest example of gamification in my work: the games existed to get a specific product capability into someone's hands, not to fill floor space.

gamificationgameslearner engagement

Camera comparison reports that set the training message

From 2025 · every new generation against the one before it · reported to management and the training team

When a new handset arrived I put it beside its predecessor — an A17 next to the A16 — and tested the cameras properly, in real conditions rather than on a spec sheet. I know photography, so I could tell the difference between a number that changed and a result a customer would actually notice.

The output was a report to managers, internal teams and the training team saying which points we should emphasise when we talk about this phone — and, just as usefully, which ones were not worth the airtime. The training message for a launch started here.

The specification pages of those reports are Samsung-internal and stay that way. The comparison pages are my own photographs, shot in my own office, and the judgement written across them is mine. The method is what transfers: test it yourself, then decide what the sales floor should say.

research & analysistechnical groundinginstructional end goalssales processes

Service tutorials, built from real support questions

Scenarios written from FAQ analysis · produced with an agency

Working with the service team, I looked at what customers were actually asking — how to charge the phone properly, how to look after the battery, how to update, how to move data across — and wrote scenarios for short tutorials answering exactly those. The agency filmed them.

The method matters more than the films: the curriculum came from support data, not from a feature list.

research on learnersinstructional end goalsscripts

Tips & Tricks films, and a 360° product format

20–30+ Tips & Tricks films over the years

Short films covering one feature at a time, with the material customised for each audience and each market rather than reused as it arrived.

Samsung produced 360-degree turntable footage of each handset for other purposes. It had a training use: re-cut in Adobe Premiere with camera specifications and feature callouts over the top, a whole product could be introduced in about a minute. That format was my idea, and I edited it.

A Fox Under a Pink Moon — coaching a film crew

Samsung-sponsored film · shot on Galaxy S21 Ultra

Samsung sponsored this film, and it was shot on the phone. As training manager I taught the lead actor how to film with it — the handling, the techniques and the camera features — so that the footage coming back would be usable.

We then reviewed the sequences together to check what the phone had actually captured.

Teaching my own colleagues

Recognised twice — Employee of the Quarter, and for knowledge sharing

Internal classes for Samsung colleagues on three subjects: using AI features on Samsung phones, running AI tools locally on your own machine rather than in the cloud, and photography with the newer Samsung cameras. The local-AI class used free software on purpose, so people could carry on afterwards without a licence.

Teaching colleagues is the part of the job I like most, and it is the closest thing in my history to advising the people who deliver training.

A recent sample

Built recently while learning Articulate Rise. It is a sample rather than a body of work, and it is here so you can see how I structure a lesson.

Selling the Camera

6 lessons · 2 scored knowledge checks with written feedback · 1 branching scenario · 1 job aid

A short module for a retail associate: demonstrate a phone camera in under two minutes. Read what the customer wants from one question, choose the single feature that answers it, hand the phone over. Written in the register of the dealer training I ran for eight years.

The content is drawn from my own curriculum — autofocus tracking taught as keeping a moving child sharp, Object Eraser and Photo Remaster on a photo the customer already owns, Director's View for someone who already films.

Built with AI assistance, which is worth saying plainly. The structure, the questions and the feedback are mine; the assembly inside Rise was done with an AI tool working to my direction. Using AI that way is deliberate, and it is what the Google AI Essentials certification was for.
